_note: One-line summaries shown in the contents lists and at the top of each page. Keyed by section/slug. Pages not listed fall back to their first paragraph.
ux/design-origins: A short history of UX, from the first stone tools and Greek theatres to the pocket watch, the industrial revolution and the internet.
ux/starting-point: Projects never start neatly. How to begin when the problem is still abstract and only fragments are visible.
ux/what-is-ux-design: UX as a philosophy built on empathy, with Walt Disney as an example of designing for how people feel.
ux/the-father-of-ux: Don Norman's core principles, starting with affordance: make it obvious what your product does.
ux/key-figures: Eleven people who shaped UX, from Daniel Kahneman and Don Norman to Shigeru Miyamoto and Walt Disney.
ux/key-roles: The jobs in a design team, from creative directors and design leads to developers and UX researchers.
ux/the-bias-of-beauty: Why symmetry and beauty make a design feel good and trustworthy, and how to use that bias.
ux/bias: Eleven cognitive biases, from authority bias to survivorship bias, and how they shape users' decisions.
ux/mental-models: How mental models shape what users expect, where bias comes from, and why recognition beats recall.
ux/laws-of-ux: Jon Yablonski's Laws of UX, from Hick's and Jakob's laws to the peak-end rule and Tesler's law.
ux/design-psychology: Gestalt psychology: how the brain finds patterns and groups what it sees, and what that means for layout.
ux/neilson-heuristics: Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristics: the rules for checking whether an interface is usable.
ux/data: Evidence-based design: what counts as data, bad and false data, qualitative vs quantitative research, and the Pepsi Challenge.
ux/what-is-design-thinking: Design thinking as a science-based problem-solving framework, and how your sprint follows it.
ux/wicked-problem: Wicked problems: complex, shifting challenges with no single answer, and why design thinking exists to tackle them.
ux/stages-of-wireframes: The iterative path from task flows and sketches to paper, low-fi, style guide and high-fi prototypes.
ux/target-mvp: Define your Minimum Viable Product, Most Valuable Person and Minimum Desirable Product to focus the sprint.
ux/gestures: The standard touch gestures on mobile and in VR, from tap and swipe to pinch and long press.
ux/haptics: Haptics: how touch and vibration give users feedback when they use technology.
ux/bad-user-experience: Real examples of bad UX, from the Willy Wonka Experience to coercive design, poor accessibility and unclear signs.
ux/a-case-of-genius: The Trunki ride-on suitcase as a case study in designing for a real user need.
ux/the-death-of-kodak: Why Kodak failed to adapt to digital, and what that teaches about rapid prototyping and design thinking.
figma/choose-your-frame: How to pick a Figma frame size for the device you'll design and prototype on, and why aspect ratio matters.
figma/starting-in-figma: Your first Figma walkthrough: set up frames, then build and style the shapes for an animated button.
figma/beginners-guide-to-grids: Set up columns, rows, gutters and margins in Figma to build a grid layout.
figma/beginners-guide-to-nesting: Nest one container inside another using grids and margins.
figma/beginners-guide-auto-layout: Use Auto Layout to build a button with padding and an icon, then turn it into a component.
figma/beginners-guide-to-8-point-grid-sy: Why spacing everything in multiples of 8 keeps layouts consistent, with a timed exercise.
figma/beginners-guide-to-components: Go from a list of components to a reusable library, and build your own.
figma/navbar: Build a navbar component from Phosphor icon sets with on and off states, then prototype it across four screens.
figma/dynamic-buttons-part-one: Build a reusable button component with text properties, appearance booleans and icon swaps.
figma/dynamic-buttons-part-deux: Turn your button into a component set with seven variants: default, hover, pressed, stroke, disabled and glass.
figma/color-variables: Create colour variables from a Grabient gradient and organise them into collections.
figma/number-variables: Record your phone's frame, content areas, gaps and radii as number variables you can reuse.
figma/string-variables: Store text in string variables and update it everywhere from one place.
figma/variable-modes: Use variable modes and a prototype interaction to switch a product's colour on hover.
ui/colour-values: The colour formats designers use, HEX, RGB, CMYK and HSL, and where each one fits.
ui/atomic-design-methodology: Brad Frost's atomic design: build interfaces from atoms and molecules up to organisms, templates and pages.
ui/file-types: When to use JPG, PNG, GIF, SVG, WEBP and TIFF in interface work.
ui/spacing-grids: A short history of grids, and how column grids, responsiveness and the 8-point system work in UI.
ui/typeface: Key type terms and the major typeface classifications, plus 11 typefaces and the stories behind them.
ui/style-guides: What a style tile or style guide is, and how it communicates colour, type and graphic styles.
ui/icons: Icon types, and how to use icons well: add labels, keep the geometry consistent and keep them simple.
ui/paper-wireframes: Sketch your UI on paper to think it through before you open Figma.
exercises/sidebar: Design a sidebar rail for Bubble, an app that helps people write film scripts.
exercises/friends-list: Design an accessible contacts list for Huddle, an app for people who meet up to play sport.
exercises/new-notification: Design a notifications panel for Fireballs, a social network for fantasy gamers.
exercises/bottom-sheet: Design a bottom sheet that confirms a money transfer for Neobank, a digital bank.
exercises/sign-in: Design a sign-in page for Nomad, a community for finding people to travel with.
exercises/cc-checkout: Design the card checkout for a sneaker shop's e-commerce app.
exercises/video-player: Design a simple, instantly recognisable video player for a streaming service.
exercises/choose-a-movie: Design a movie trailer intro page for a streaming service that invites people to press play.
exercises/music-player: Design the paused screen of Bop, a new music streaming app.
exercises/home-monitor-dash: Design a modular dashboard for a smart-home monitoring app.
exercises/user-profile-page: Design a profile page that presents personal and professional details in a clean, usable layout.
exercises/make-an-ai-interface: Design an AI assistant interface that feels smart and human but still matches what users expect.
exercises/product-card: Design a product card that showcases a wallpaper in an online shop or magazine.
exercises/ux-x-ai: Use AI tools to help you design, prototype and test an app idea in one afternoon.
exercises/airbnb-replica-challenge: Trace seven real Airbnb screens in Figma, from the first notification prompt to Confirm and pay: by hand first, then with Auto Layout and components.
exercises/glovo-replica-challenge: Recreate the Glovo app screen by screen in Figma: by hand first, then rebuilt with Auto Layout and components.
exercises/youtube-challenge: Recreate the YouTube app screen by screen in Figma: by hand first, then rebuilt with Auto Layout and components.
exercises/stage-play: As a team, build the Stage Play app in Figma from a component schema, using master components, nesting, auto layout and properties.
methods/lean-ux-canvas: Frame the problem as a team: the business outcome, the users and the value they'll get.
methods/long-term-goal: Agree the best-case future for your users, so every sprint decision has a direction.
methods/research-goal: Write down what you want to learn before you start researching.
methods/research-questions: Turn your research goal into specific, open questions that guide the research.
methods/user-survey: Design an unbiased survey to gather evidence from people's real experiences.
methods/user-interview: Interview users to uncover the why behind what they do and need.
methods/discovery-summary: Pull your research together into key insights, surprises and next steps.
methods/problem-statement: Write a short, solution-free description of the main problem users face.
methods/user-persona: Turn your research into an evidence-based persona of your target user.
methods/competitive-analysis: Study 3–5 competitors to find gaps and ideas for your design.
methods/how-might-we: List the ways your project could fail, then flip them into 'How might we…' opportunities.
methods/pick-a-target: Choose your Minimum Viable Product, Most Valuable Person and Minimum Desirable Product.
methods/user-journey-map: Map the user's steps, feelings and pain points as they work towards a goal.
methods/task-flows: Break the main task into the fewest steps a user needs, drawn as a simple flow.
methods/crazy-8s: Sketch eight different ideas in eight minutes to get past your first idea.
methods/crazy-8s-with-ai: Crazy 8's with AI as a sparring partner, suggesting variations for you to sketch.
methods/solution-sketch: Present your solution sketch to the team, gallery-style, and discuss it.
methods/converge-diverge: Decide as a team whether to combine ideas into one prototype or test competing ones.
methods/vote: Vote on the sketches to choose which ideas to take forward.
methods/mood-board: Collect colours, type, imagery and textures to explore the look and feel.
methods/style-guide: Turn your mood board into a practical guide: logo, type, colours, icons and buttons.
methods/paper-wireframes: Sketch your main task flow on paper, focusing on structure, not polish.
methods/desk-research: Gather what is already known about your problem from credible sources, then decide what your own research must find out.
methods/site-visit: Go to the place where the problem happens and observe quietly, to pick up cues users would never mention.
methods/affinity-mapping: Sort research findings into clusters on sticky notes, name the themes and agree what matters most.
methods/data-synthesis-with-ai: Use AI for a first pass at coding your research notes, then check every suggestion against the raw data.
methods/business-model-canvas: Describe how the idea creates, delivers and captures value in nine blocks on one page.
methods/wicked-problem-mapping: Map a wicked problem as a web of causes and actors, then find one leverage point small enough to design for.
methods/service-design-blueprint: Map one journey from the customer's actions down to the backstage processes that make it happen.
methods/dvf-analysis: Score ideas for desirability, viability and feasibility, then rank and discuss them as a team.
methods/sitemap: Draw the hierarchy of every page in your site or app, and check it for gaps and pages buried too deep.
methods/mood-board-with-ai: Generate, react and refine visuals with AI in loops, then build a mood board around your mood words.
methods/brand-pack: Turn your mood board into an identity: name, logo, colour, type, imagery and tone of voice.
methods/ab-test: Compare two versions of a screen that differ in one way, on task success and preference, and decide with evidence.
methods/cataloguing-artifacts: Gather, label and sort every artifact from your projects, and choose the strongest for your case studies.
methods/process-narrative: Write a case study as a story in four beats: purpose, challenges, when things got tough, and reflection.
methods/mid-fi: Rebuild your paper wireframes as greyscale mid-fi screens with the Figma Mid-Fi kit or Miro, only for the screens you need.
methods/hi-fi: Turn your wireframes into a polished, clickable Figma prototype with real content.
methods/usability-test: Plan and run five usability tests, then find the patterns in what users did.
methods/create-your-script: Write and rehearse the script you'll follow when testing with users.
methods/facilitator-format: How the facilitator runs a test: welcome, context, objective, thinking aloud and the debrief.
methods/limited-intervention-technique: Don't lead users during a test: give clues, not answers.
methods/notetaker-format: What the note-taker watches for: what users say and do, and what they think and feel.
methods/design-iteration: Turn test findings into 2–3 design changes, shown as before-and-after snapshots.
methods/sprint-retrospective: Reflect on what worked, what didn't and what you learned. It becomes the first page of your case study.
